Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Open Port is the technical term for the most common vulnerability in any network. The brand sits on the technical reality the customer already lives with. Modern, immediately legible to the audience, and slightly ironic: we are the company that closes them.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern cybersecurity has split into two camps: the giant legacy vendors (Symantec, McAfee) and the modern product-led players (Wiz, SentinelOne, Snyk). The customer is a CISO or security engineer who already evaluates five vendors a quarter and wants the sixth to be the one that actually works.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Wiz (wiz.io) holds the modern cloud-security peer position. SentinelOne (sentinelone.com) sits in the endpoint tier. Snyk (snyk.io) does the developer-led security middle. CrowdStrike (crowdstrike.com) is the institutional peer. We sit closest to Wiz in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: Cloud security that ships findings developers will actually fix.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most security products ship noise. We ship findings prioritized by exploitability and fixability. The brand promise is that the security team's first list of findings can be triaged in an afternoon.

targetAudience.primary: CISOs, Heads of Security, and Security Engineers at companies of 200 to 10000 employees. They already use three security tools and want the fourth to consolidate the stack.

dos: Show the finding and the fix side by side
Lead with what the product ships
Speak to the security engineer who'd use the tool

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. OPEN PORT in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, two opposing brackets suggesting a port closing, used as the favicon and on the security dashboard.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No 'nation-state threats' marketing. No glowing-figure-in-hoodie illustrations. No fear-based ad campaigns. No founder podcast about cyber warfare.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A landing page that shows a real finding in the first scroll. A product dashboard that prioritizes findings by exploitability. A changelog written like a developer talking to other developers.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Three words. Wellesley sounds like an old English firm. & Co. closes it as a small heritage advisory. The whole name reads like a quiet security consultancy serving a small set of clients who would never call themselves clients.
Luxury.story: Wellesley & Co. began with two principals who had spent decades inside intelligence services and major security firms, and wanted to take fewer clients, more carefully. The firm accepts a limited number of engagements each year. Most clients are second or third generation family offices, foundations, or institutions.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end security advisory has been consolidating into large consulting firms with quarterly earnings calls. There's a parallel market for small principal-led firms with deep client relationships, where the work is sensitive and the engagement is long. The customer is paying for the principals, the discretion, and the long-term relationship.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Kroll (kroll.com) holds the institutional security consulting peer. Control Risks (controlrisks.com) sits at the international tier. K2 Integrity (k2integrity.com) does the financial-services-led middle. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small advisory firm providing strategic security counsel to families, foundations, and institutions.

targetAudience.primary: Family offices, foundations, private trustees, and institutions with multi-generational counsel needs. Often inherited the relationship. Values the discretion above all.

dos: Speak in the language of the discipline

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the firm's hallmark, used on letterhead, the brass plaque outside the office, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

colorPalette.name: Counsel Green
colorPalette.meaning: Old library walls, the partner's room.

typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the secure portal.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No public client list. No press appearances. No conference speaking. No social media. No content strategy. No website beyond a single address card.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Lock is the universal word for what security does. The brand sits on the most basic, useful word in the category. Plain, direct, immediately understood.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most cybersecurity brands have elaborate names suggesting threat, defense, or military origin. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the simplest verb.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most cybersecurity brands fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some Unix-philosophy security tools and certain open-source firewall projects.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Network security. Plain product. Clear pricing.

targetAudience.primary: Engineers and small business owners who need a network firewall or endpoint protection and don't want to read sales materials. They want the product, the price, and the documentation.

dos: Show the product, the technical specs, the price
Confirm orders in one short line

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. LOCK in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, four letters with generous space. No icon. The dashboard, the documentation, and the invoice all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

typography.rationale: One face. The product, the docs, and the website all carry the same wordmark.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No threat-intelligence content. No fear-based marketing. No conference circuit. No social media presence beyond a single archive page.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Aegis is the Greek word for shield, suggesting protection. Cyber Group names the holding-company category. The whole name reads like a real, established cybersecurity holding company already on the procurement panel at major enterprises.
Corporate.industrySummary: Enterprise cybersecurity services is a multi-billion-dollar B2B category. CISOs and Heads of Security want partners who can deliver detection, response, and compliance at enterprise scale. The category is mostly served by the giant integrators and a few specialist firms.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Mandiant, now part of Google Cloud (cloud.google.com/security/mandiant) holds the institutional incident-response peer. Booz Allen Hamilton (boozallen.com) sits at the government-meets-enterprise tier. Optiv (optiv.com) is the channel-led peer. We sit smaller, focused on mid-market and contemporary enterprise.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Cybersecurity services for mid-market and growth-stage enterprise.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Mid-market and growth-stage companies are too small for Mandiant attention and too sophisticated for boutique firms. We sit between them, with operating discipline and modern delivery.

targetAudience.primary: CISOs, Chief Information Officers, and Heads of Security at companies of 500 to 10000 employees. They sign multi-year contracts.

customSections.body: No D2C security product. No free consumer tools. No celebrity-CISO partnerships. The firm sells through enterprise procurement, not security-conference theatre.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Patch Notes is the software-industry term for the changelog of fixes shipped in a release. The brand puts the fix in the brand position, not the threat. Loud, slightly cheeky, and immediately legible to the developer-and-security audience.
Creative.manifesto: Most cybersecurity brands sell fear. The breach, the threat, the nation-state actor. We made Patch Notes because the actual work of security is mostly fixing things, one at a time, in a long quiet list. We sell the fix. We sell the changelog. We are not a fear brand. We are a maintenance brand.
Creative.industrySummary: Cybersecurity branding has been polished, fear-based, and slightly cold. There's room for a brand that's warm, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about the actual maintenance work that keeps systems secure.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Tailscale (tailscale.com) does warm-technical security well. 1Password (1password.com) holds the design-led consumer position. Cloudflare (cloudflare.com) does the infrastructure peer. We sit warmer and more honest about the work than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A security brand for the people doing the maintenance.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Security engineers, DevOps engineers, IT operations managers. They already use three security tools and want the fourth to be the one their team actually likes.

dos: Show the patch and what it fixed
Make jokes about the security industry
Talk like the engineer who'd be implementing the fix

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display sans with the T of NOTES stylized as a small cross or fix symbol. Standalone fix-cross icon for stickers, social profiles, and the back of every release email.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a fear brand. Not a nation-state-threats brand. Not afraid of green. Not too cool to celebrate fixing a CVE.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A weekly newsletter that's actually patch notes from the team. Stickers in every welcome envelope. A merch line of two tees that say PATCH NOTES across the back. A small in-person meetup for security engineers every quarter.
